note.explanation: A physical balance measures mass by comparing an object with known standard masses. Put the object on the left pan and standard masses on the right pan. When the pointer stays at zero or oscillates equally on both sides of zero, add the standard masses to find the object's mass.
examples: If the balance is level when a 20 g mass and a 5 g mass are on the right pan, the object on the left pan has a mass of 25 g.
A spring balance measures weight, which is a force; a physical balance is used to compare masses.
note.checkAnswer: The total of the standard masses on the right pan is the mass of the object on the left pan.
note.simple: A physical balance finds mass by balancing an object against known masses.
note.checkQuestion: When the pointer is balanced, how do you find the object's mass?
note.title: Measuring Mass with a Physical Balance
steps: Level the base using the levelling screws until the plumb line is exactly above the pointed mark.
Raise the pans and make sure the beam is horizontal and the pointer is at the centre of the scale. Adjust the balancing screws if needed.
Place the object on the left pan.
Use forceps to place known masses from the weight box on the right pan.
Adjust the masses until the pointer stays on zero or oscillates equally on both sides of zero.
Add the standard masses on the right pan. Their total is the mass of the object.
note.answer: The total of the standard masses on the right pan gives the mass of the object on the left pan.

steps.why: The balance must be level before its readings can be used.
steps.text: Level base of the balance using levelling screws until the plumb line is exactly above the pointed mark.

steps.why: The unloaded balance should be adjusted so its beam and pointer show the correct starting position.
steps.text: Turn the knob so that the pans of the balance are raised up. Is the beam horizontal and pointer at the centre of the scale? If not, turn the balancing screws on the beam so that it becomes horizontal.

steps.why: The object is placed on the pan specified for weighing it.
steps.text: Place the object to be weighed on the left pan.

steps.why: Known masses provide the standard for comparison.
steps.text: Place the known weight from the weight box in the right pan using forceps.

steps.why: A zero position or equal oscillations show that the two sides are balanced.
steps.text: Adjust the weight so that pointer remains on zero or oscillates equally on both sides of the zero of the scale.

steps.why: At balance, the total of the known masses gives the object's mass.
steps.text: The total of standard masses (weights) is a measure of the mass of the object in the left pan.

example.question: How is the mass of an object measured using a physical balance?
example.answer: Level and adjust the balance, put the object on the left pan, and add known masses to the right pan until the pointer is balanced. The total of the standard masses is the mass of the object.

explain.title: Mass and weight are different
explain.body: Mass is the measure of quantity of matter in a body whereas the weight is the force by which the body is attracted towards the Earth. Weight can be measured using spring balance.

explain.title: What weighing means
explain.body: The mass of an object is found by comparing it with known standard masses. This process is called weighing.

explain.title: How a physical balance works
explain.body: In laboratories, we use physical balance shown in Fig. 1.9 which is based on the principle of levers. The object is placed in one pan and known masses are added to the other pan until they balance.

explain.title: Read the balance carefully
explain.body: The pointer should remain on zero or oscillate equally on both sides of the zero of the scale. The total of standard masses (weights) is a measure of the mass of the object in the left pan.

mistakes: Do not call mass and weight the same thing: the textbook defines mass as quantity of matter and weight as a force.
Do not put the object and the standard masses in the same pan; the object goes on the left and the known masses go on the right.
Do not use your fingers to place the known masses; the procedure specifies using forceps.
Do not take the mass reading before checking the pointer. The pointer must stay on zero or oscillate equally on both sides.
Do not forget to add the standard masses to obtain the object's mass.
